Abstract: We conducted the current review of the paraneo-
plastic neurologic syndromes (PNSs) associated with gynecologic
and breast carcinomas to describe their clinical and immunologic
characteristics and their relative frequency. We retrospectively re-
viewed 92 patients whose serum was sent to our laboratories to de-
tect onconeural antibodies and who were diagnosed as having
PNSs associated with breast or gynecologic tumors. PNSs were de-
ﬁned as “deﬁnitive” and “possible” (atypical PNS, no onconeural
antibodies, and no improvement after tumor treatment). Forty-
nine patients had breast and 43 had gynecologic cancer. Sixty-three
patients had onconeural antibodies (50 Yo-ab, 5 Hu-ab, 5 Ri-ab,
and 3 amphiphysin-ab). Cerebellar ataxia represented 57 (62%) of
all PNSs and was associated with anti-Yo in 88%. All Yo-ab-
negative patients had breast cancer; 4 of them had a mild cerebel-
lar syndrome that improved after tumor treatment. Sensory-
predominant neuropathies were present in 17 (18%) patients. Seven
of them had Hu-ab (5) or amphiphysin-ab (2). Other PNSs were op-
soclonus-myoclonus syndrome (4 cases, Ri-ab in 2), sensorimotor
neuropathy (4 cases), paraneoplastic encephalomyelitis (4 cases, Ri-
ab in 3), paraneoplastic retinopathy (2 cases), amyotrophic lateral
sclerosis (2 cases), stiff-person syndrome (1 with amphiphysin-ab),
and limbic encephalitis (1 case). All patients with gynecologic can-
cer presented deﬁnitive PNS, and onconeural antibodies were di-
agnosed in 93% of them. In contrast, 20% of PNSs associated with
breast cancer were deﬁned as possible and the incidence of onco-
neural antibodies was 51%, excluding the 2 patients with paraneo-
plastic retinopathy in whom antiretinal antibodies were not ana-
lyzed. In patients with possible PNS, a coincidental association
between the tumor and the neurologic disorder cannot be ex-
cluded.
(Medicine 2003;82: 216–23)
INTRODUCTION
P
araneoplastic neurologic syndromes (PNSs) are deﬁned
as neurologic syndromes of unclear cause that prefer-
entially occur in patients with an underlying, usually oc-
cult, neoplasm (49). Gynecologic and breast carcinomas
are, after small cell lung cancer, the group of solid tumors
most frequently associated with PNSs (14, 49). The range
and relative frequency of the different PNSs related to
small cell lung cancer are known (49); the 2 most frequent
are the Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome (44) and the
different clinical syndromes included in the term “paraneo-
plastic encephalomyelitis associated with anti-Hu antibod-
ies (Hu-ab)” (23, 37). However, this information is less
clear for gynecologic and breast carcinomas. Earlier, au-
thors emphasized the presence of peripheral neuropathies
(14). However, more recent studies suggest that the most
frequent PNS is paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration as-
sociated with anti-Yo antibodies (Yo-ab) (45).
In the present study, we reviewed the PNSs related
to breast and gynecologic carcinomas identiﬁed in 2 refer-
ence centers to learn the distribution and relative fre-
quency of the different PNSs and to identify possible new
clinical-immunologic associations. 
METHODS
Patients
Patients included in this study were selected from those
whose serum or cerebrospinal ﬂuid (CSF) samples were sent to 2
laboratories (Hospital Clínic, Barcelona, and Hôpital de la
Salpêtrière, Paris) for detection of onconeural antibodies. Both

laboratories are reference centers in their own countries and
therefore no particular bias on referral pattern should be ex-
pected other than those PNSs known to be associated with spe-
ciﬁc antineuronal antibodies. Occasionally, we also receive sam-
ples from other European countries and from other laboratories
concerning cases of special clinical or immunologic interest. 
The methods to detect onconeural antibodies have been
described in detail previously (22, 60). Brieﬂy, a preliminary
screening was done incubating the serum or CSF with frozen sec-
tions of rat cerebellum. Samples with immunohistochemical pat-
terns suggestive of onconeural antibodies (Hu, Yo, Ri, Tr, CV2,
amphiphysin) were conﬁrmed by immunoblot of neuronal ex-

identiﬁed by the immunoreactivity pattern alone because the im-
munoblot is negative (22). Antirecoverin (48) and anti-Ma anti-
bodies (52) were not evaluated in the present series. Antibody
titers were not obtained. A serum was considered positive if the
antibody reactivity was demonstrated at the screening serum di-
lution (1:500).
Inclusion criteria
Patients were included in the study based on the following
criteria:
1) If they had a pathologic diagnosis of gynecologic or
breast cancer, or only radiologic evidence in patients
with typical onconeural antibodies, or regional
adenopathies with suggestive pathology of breast or
ovarian cancer, in the absence of a demonstrable pri-
mary tumor; and 
2) if they presented 1 of the following: 
a) a typical onconeural antibody, or 
b) they were seronegative but met all of the following
criteria: 
i) latency between neurologic syndrome and tu-
mor diagnosis less than 4 years. (The follow-up
time was based on the observation that all pa-
tients with paraneoplastic Lambert-Eaton myas-
thenic syndrome developed small cell lung can-
cer within 4 years [44]), 
ii) adequate clinical and radiologic information to
deﬁne a speciﬁc neurologic syndrome, and
iii) absence of another diagnosis that could explain
the neurologic disorder.
We recognize that patients included in the seronegative
group could have true paraneoplastic syndromes or coincidental
association of idiopathic neurologic disorders and cancer. To
clarify this issue, PNS patients were grouped in 2 different cate-
gories according to the level of paraneoplastic evidence:
1) Deﬁnitive PNS: patients with a neurologic syndrome
not explained by other causes and positive onconeural
antibodies, or patients without onconeural antibodies
and either a typical paraneoplastic neurologic syn-
drome (sensory neuropathy, paraneoplastic cerebellar
degeneration, limbic encephalitis, cancer-associated
retinopathy, stiff-person syndrome, opsoclonus-
myoclonus syndrome, Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syn-
drome) or other neurologic syndrome that improved
after tumor treatment.
2) Possible PNS: patients without onconeural antibodies
in whom the neurologic disorder did not have a typical
PNS clinical picture and who did not improve after tu-
mor treatment.
Selection methods 
We retrospectively selected all patients from our databases
who fulﬁlled the inclusion criteria described above (47 patients
from Barcelona; 30 patients from Paris). In addition we under-
took 2 approaches to update the clinical information with 
contact by phone and written questionnaires to the referring neu-
rologists: 1) in the Hospital Clínic we contacted the referring
neurologists of 68 seronegative women without cancer when
their samples were analyzed between 1994 and 2000. We se-
lected only patients in whom the initial clinical information re-
sembled any of the typical PNSs described above. After the sur-
vey, 7 of the 68 patients were considered to have a PNS.
Complete information was not available for 24 of the 68 patients,
as we could not contact the referring physician, or no informa-
tion about the patient was provided. 2) In the Hôpital de la
Salpêtrière, 180 seronegative women without cancer when their
serum was analyzed between 1997 and 1999 were reevaluated re-
gardless of the neurologic syndrome. A clinical update was ob-
tained in 167 patients, and 8 met the previously deﬁned criteria

for PNSs. After the survey, we had a total of 92 patients with de-
ﬁnitive or possible PNS and cancer of breast or gynecologic ori-
gin (54 patients from Barcelona; 38 patients from Paris).
RESULTS
The clinical and immunologic characteristics of the 92
patients are summarized in Table 1. Forty-nine patients had
breast cancer and 43 had cancer of gynecologic origin (35
ovary, 3 uterus, 3 fallopian tube, and 2 cervix). Two patients
with Yo-ab had a radiologic diagnosis suspicious of ovarian
cancer, and 3 presented retroperitoneal adenopathies, the
histology of which was suggestive of ovarian origin. In 6 pa-
tients, the diagnosis of breast cancer was provided by biopsy
of an axillary adenopathy in the absence of a primary tumor
(1 Hu-ab, 1 amphiphysin-ab, and 4 seronegative). 
Clinical picture
Cerebellar syndrome 
A cerebellar syndrome was present in 57 (62%) of the
92 patients. Fifty of them were positive for Yo-ab and al-
most all had a subacute, severe, and irreversible pancere-
bellar syndrome (45, 51). The other 7 patients, all with
breast cancer, did not have any onconeural antibody
(Table 2). In 2 of them, the clinical syndrome was indis-
tinguishable from that of Yo-ab-associated paraneoplastic
cerebellar degeneration. Patient 1 was a 47-year-old woman
who presented with a subacute, severe pancerebellar syn-
drome. Brain magnetic resonance (MR) was normal and
CSF analysis showed 40 white cells. Two months later, an
adenocarcinoma of probable breast origin was demon-
strated in an axillary adenopathy. Four years later, she was
tumor free but very disabled from the cerebellar syndrome.
Patient 2 was a 42-year-old woman who developed a severe
cerebellar syndrome 1 month after diagnosis of breast can-
cer. Brain MR was normal and CSF analysis showed 10
white cells. Two years later, she was tumor free and neuro-
logically stable. 
Among the other 5 patients, 4 presented a favorable
evolution related to treatment of the tumor (see Table 2,

Patients 4, 5, 6, 7). These patients had a mild to moderate

sis of breast cancer. They all had normal MR, and the cere-
bellar syndrome improved after removal of the tumor.
Patient 3 (see Table 2) was considered to be possibly para-
neoplastic as she did not improve after tumor treatment.
She had cerebellar atrophy in the initial MR and the clin-
ical picture was similar to that of idiopathic cerebellar de-
generation. 
Sensory-predominant neuropathy
We included in this group 17 (18%) patients in whom
sensory symptoms were the initial complaint and re-
mained isolated or clearly predominant during most of the
clinical course. Patients who showed minor motor weak-
ness or only neurophysiologic motor involvement were in-
cluded in this group. Five patients were positive for Hu-ab
(3 breast, 2 ovary), 2 had amphyphisin-ab (2 breast), 1 had
an atypical antibody (ovary), and 9 had no detectable
antibodies (7 breast, 1 ovary, 1 cervix). The clinical picture
of those patients with Hu-ab, atypical antibody, and
amphiphysin-ab resembled that of patients with Hu-ab,
small cell lung cancer, and sensory neuropathy with pre-
dominant involvement of vibratory and joint position
senses and asymmetric onset (41). The serum of the patient
with the atypical antibody immunoreacted with the neu-
ronal cytoplasm in a pattern different from that described
in a patient with chronic, asymmetric, ataxic sensory neu-
ropathy and breast cancer, whose serum reacted with the
posterior gray horn of the spinal cord (30). All the seropos-
itive patients had an isolated sensory neuropathy with clin-
ical features (asymmetric onset, early involvement of
hands, sensory ataxia) and electromyography (EMG) fea-
tures (absent sensory nerve action potentials with normal
motor nerve conduction velocities in the 5 studies re-
viewed) compatible with primary involvement of the dor-
sal root ganglia (neuronopathy) (13).
The clinical picture and evolution of the 9 seronega-
tive patients was heterogeneous (Table 3). Five patients
(see Table 3, Patients 1, 5, 6, 7, 8) had a large ﬁber sensory
neuropathy with predominant gait ataxia. Four of them
had atypical features for seropositive sensory neuropathy,
2 patients improved, another developed a severe motor
deﬁcit over the ensuing years, and 1 patient had a demy-
elinating neuropathy. Two patients (see Table 3, Patients 3
and 4) presented with paresthesias and itching in the lower
limbs 5 and 9 months before breast cancer was diagnosed
(46). Lastly, Patients 2 and 9 were considered to have pos-
sible paraneoplastic sensory neuropathy because they had
less speciﬁc sensory symptoms (numbness and paresthe-
sias) and did not improve after treatment of the tumor.
Sensorimotor neuropathy
Four patients (4.3%) presented with peripheral neu-
ropathy and predominant motor impairment considered to
be possible PNS associated with breast cancer. Two patients
developed an acute sensorimotor neuropathy fulﬁlling the
criteria for Guillain Barré syndrome, 1 coincident with and
the other 4 months after diagnosis of breast cancer. Two pa-
tients presented a neuropathy with the features of chronic id-
iopathic demyelinating polyneuropathy 9 months before
and 5 months after the diagnosis of breast cancer, respec-
tively. EMG studies suggested a chronic demyelinating
polyradiculoneuropathy in both patients, and a nerve biopsy
performed in 1 demonstrated inﬂammatory and demyelin-

ating features. CSF analysis showed elevated protein content
in both (0.53 and 1.20 g/L, respectively), and hypercellular-
ity in 1 (19 white cells with 84% lymphocytes). Clinical evo-
lution was progressive in 1 and remitting-relapsing in the
other. Both patients responded to plasmapheresis.

Opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome
Four patients presented with opsoclonus-myoclonus
syndrome. Three patients had breast cancer (2 with Ri-ab)
and 1 ovarian carcinoma. No clinical differences were ob-
served between Ri-ab-negative and Ri-ab-positive patients
with breast cancer. The patient with ovarian cancer devel-
oped opsoclonus without myoclonus 2 months after tumor
diagnosis and after a second cycle of carboplatin, taxol,
and topotecan. The syndrome did not improve and the pa-
tient died from tumor progression 4 months later.
Other neurologic syndromes
Seven patients were considered to have deﬁnitive
PNS associated with breast cancer. Three patients pre-
sented with multifocal involvement of the nervous system
(encephalomyelitis) associated with Ri-ab. Two of them
had a predominant brainstem syndrome with ophthal-
moparesis, dysarthria, tremor, and axial or pancerebellar
syndrome but no opsoclonus. Dorsal bulboprotuberantial,
bilateral, and symmetric hyperintense lesions on T2-
weighted MR images were observed in 1 of the patients.
The third Ri-ab-positive patient presented with a progres-
sive paraparesia with abolished deep tendon reﬂexes and
a T9 sensory level. She subsequently developed weakness
in the upper limbs, urinary incontinence, dysarthria, and
postural tremor in the head and both arms. EMG showed
denervation in the 4 limbs without bulbar involvement.
Spinal and brain MR were normal. A breast adenocarci-
noma was diagnosed 8 months after the onset of neuro-
logic symptoms. 
Two patients had cancer-associated retinopathy.
Antirecoverin or other antiretinal antibodies were not
measured. One patient developed a typical stiff-person
syndrome (positive for amphiphysin-ab, negative for
GAD-ab), and another presented with limbic encephalitis
deﬁned by clinical and MR features 3 months before the
diagnosis of breast cancer. 
Lastly, 3 seronegative patients with breast cancer
were considered as possible paraneoplastic. Two had
amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. The third patient presented
a subacute cerebellar syndrome with multicranial nerve in-
volvement (right VI and VII and bilateral XII nerve
palsies) and bilateral Babinski sign. An axillary lymph
node biopsy revealed an adenocarcinoma 2 months after
the onset of the neurologic symptoms. Distal paresthesias
and amyotrophy appeared during evolution, and elec-
trophysiologic studies revealed an axonal sensory-
predominant neuropathy. She did not improve after treat-
ment of the tumor.
In summary, all patients with gynecologic cancer
presented with deﬁnitive PNS, and onconeural antibodies
were diagnosed in 93% of them. In contrast, 20% of PNSs
associated with breast cancer were deﬁned as possible and
the incidence of onconeural antibodies was 51%, exclud-
ing the 2 patients with paraneoplastic retinopathy in whom
antiretinal antibodies were not analyzed.
DISCUSSION 
In the current study we conﬁrm the previous im-
pression that paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration is the
most frequent PNS in patients with breast and gynecologic
cancer and show sensory-predominant neuropathy to be
the second most frequent PNS, a feature not, to our knowl-
edge, previously recognized. We also found that 20% of
PNSs could be classiﬁed only as “possible” in the breast
cancer group. This observation should be expected. The
higher incidence of breast cancer compared with that of
gynecologic tumors makes more possible the coincidence
of 2 diseases that may not be related to each other.

The methodology of our study has several limita-
tions. Clinical follow-up could not be obtained in 15% of
the seronegative patients in whom additional information
was requested to see if the neurologic syndrome was para-
neoplastic, so the frequency of antibody-negative PNS
may be higher than the 31% of the study. Dermatomyosi-
tis, a classical PNS associated with breast and ovarian
cancer (7), was not included in this study because these pa-
tients are not investigated for onconeural antibodies. How-
ever, the frequency of dermatomyositis is probably lower
than that of paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration in this
population. In an epidemiologic study (56) in Sweden over
10 years, only 18 cases of dermatomyositis were detected
associated with breast or ovarian cancer.
Sensorimotor neuropathies have a much lower prob-
ability of having a paraneoplastic origin compared with
large ﬁber sensory neuropathies (50), so neurologists prob-
ably ask for the evaluation of onconeural antibodies less
frequently. However, the number of case reports of para-
neoplastic sensorimotor neuropathy associated with breast
or gynecologic cancer is low (9) (see below), if we exclude
cases of mild sensorimotor neuropathy in patients with al-
ready known, advanced tumors (12). Therefore, we do not
think our survey method has missed a substantial number
of patients with a ﬁnal diagnosis of paraneoplastic sensori-
motor neuropathy associated with these neoplasms. 
Yo-ab were identiﬁed in 88% of patients with para-
neoplastic cerebellar degeneration (100% of patients with
gynecologic cancer). Yo-ab are excellent diagnostic mark-
ers in paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration of an under-
lying breast or gynecologic cancer, with a few exceptions
(19, 24, 36, 40, 58). We previously reported 3 patients with
Yo-ab and no tumor (51). However, 2 of these patients
later developed uterine and breast cancer, 4.5 and 10 years
after the onset of paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration,
respectively. Although Yo-ab were reported in isolated
cases of polyneuropathy (35), limbic encephalitis (47), and

amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (33) associated with gyneco-

All Yo-ab-negative paraneoplastic cerebellar degen-
eration occurred in patients with breast cancer, and 2 had
a severe irreversible course as expected in Yo-ab-positive
patients. However, 4 of them had nondisabling cerebellar
ataxia that improved after treatment of the tumor. To our
knowledge this clinical evolution was not previously de-
scribed in patients with breast cancer, and resembles the
pattern seen in some patients with paraneoplastic cerebel-
lar degeneration associated with Hodgkin disease (26).
This observation conﬁrms previous work that seronegative
paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration patients comprise
a heterogeneous clinical group (2).
In the current series the second most frequent PNSs
were sensory-predominant neuropathies, which ac-
counted for 18% of all patients. When associated with on-
coneural antibodies, the clinical picture was that of large
ﬁber sensory neuropathy with a subacute nonremitting
course identical to that observed in patients with lung can-
cer and compatible with sensory neuronopathy (23). Five
seropositive patients had Hu-ab and 2 had amphiphysin-
ab. Amphiphysin-ab were initially diagnosed in patients
with stiff-person syndrome and breast cancer (20). How-
ever, they were later reported in association with various
PNSs, including paraneoplastic sensory neuropathy, and
different types of tumors, mainly small cell lung cancer and
ovary (3, 54). By contrast, CV2-ab (5), also designated
CRMP-5-ab (62), which are markers of several PNSs asso-
ciated with small cell lung cancer, have not been reported
in neuropathies related to gynecologic cancer in the cur-
rent or previous series except for a single patient with a
predominant sensory neuropathy associated with a uterine
sarcoma (5). 
In our series, seronegative patients with sensory-
predominant neuropathy showed a more heterogeneous
evolution than patients with onconeural antibodies. Two
of these seronegative patients with breast cancer presented
with itching and 1 also with cramps, resembling those pa-
tients previously described by Peterson and colleagues
(46). These authors reported 9 patients with breast cancer
and a neuropathy characterized by paresthesias and
numbness, itching, and cramps. The neuropathy had a
chronic course and did not cause a severe disability (46). 
Sensorimotor neuropathy is rarely associated with
breast cancer and much less often with gynecologic tumors
(15, 42, 46, 57, 61). Our 4 patients with sensorimotor neu-
ropathy fulﬁlled the established criteria for Guillain-Barré
syndrome or chronic inﬂammatory demyelinating poly-
neuropathy. The patients had no distinct laboratory or
clinical features to suggest a paraneoplastic origin, and
none of them was considered as deﬁnitively paraneoplas-
tic according to our deﬁnition. Authors of previous series
(4, 57) of peripheral neuropathy and cancer did not ﬁnd
cases of Guillain-Barré syndrome or chronic inﬂammatory
demyelinating polyneuropathy associated with breast or
gynecologic cancer. However, the ﬁrst series of patients
with sensorimotor neuropathy and cancer found 18% of
them associated with breast or gynecologic cancer (15).
Two patients had mild terminal neuropathies, but the
other 4 presented a remitting or relapsing course reminis-

cent of Guillain-Barré syndrome or chronic inﬂammatory
demyelinating polyneuropathy (15).
In the current series, 10% of patients presented with
PNSs, other than paraneoplastic cerebellar degeneration,
that involved the central nervous system. All but 1 had
breast cancer and 55% (5 of 9 patients) had Ri-ab. Al-
though Ri-ab were initially described in patients with op-
soclonus and breast or gynecologic cancer (32, 39), pa-
tients with Ri-ab may present with a subacute brainstem
syndrome without opsoclonus or multifocal involvement
of the central nervous system without predominant brain-
stem signs (18, 37). On the other hand, it is worthy to un-
derscore that patients with typical opsoclonus-myoclonus
syndrome and breast cancer may be Ri-ab negative (8).
One of our Ri-ab-positive patients without opsoclonus had
a brainstem lesion seen in the MR scan, an unusual ﬁnd-
ing in these patients. Similar midbrain and pontine lesions
have been reported in patients with opsoclonus and ocular
ﬂutter (11, 28, 55) from different etiologies. 
Limbic encephalitis is usually associated with small
cell lung cancer, while breast cancer is the underlying tu-
mor in 5% of patients (25). Gynecologic cancers are an un-
usual cause of limbic encephalitis, and almost half of the
reported cases were immature ovarian teratomas (25).
Limbic encephalitis does not present speciﬁc onconeural
antibodies when associated with breast or gynecologic can-
cer, but recently 2 patients with breast and 1 with ovarian
cancer presented antibodies to Ma proteins (52). 
Subacute visual loss of paraneoplastic origin in pa-
tients with breast or gynecologic tumors may be due to op-
tic neuritis (53), diffuse bilateral melanocytic proliferation
(21), and paraneoplastic retinopathy (31). Although our 2
patients with paraneoplastic retinopathy had breast cancer,
this complication usually has been described with en-
dometrial or cervix carcinomas with small cell or highly un-
differentiated features and antirecoverin antibodies (10, 16,
27, 43, 59). In contrast, the few patients reported with para-
neoplastic retinopathy and breast cancer presented with an-
tiretinal antibodies different from recoverin (1, 29, 34). 
No patient from our series had Lambert-Eaton myas-
thenic syndrome. Only a few cases of Lambert-Eaton
myasthenic syndrome and breast cancer have been re-
ported (6, 17, 44). In some of these patients the paraneo-

plastic origin of this association may be questioned due to
a long delay between Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syn-
drome and tumor diagnosis; in others, however, it should
be supported by the coincidence with dermatomyositis or
polymyositis. The low frequency of Lambert-Eaton myas-
thenic syndrome probably reﬂects absence of P/Q type
voltage gated calcium channels in the tumor or inability to
mount an immune response against this antigen. 
In conclusion, our study conﬁrms that cerebellar de-
generation is the most frequent PNS in patients with breast
or gynecologic tumors. In this setting, only a few patients
with cerebellar degeneration are Yo-ab negative. The sec-
ond most frequent PNSs were sensory-predominant neu-
ropathies, a ﬁnding not previously recognized, to our
knowledge. In breast cancer, the clinical and immunologic
spectrum of PNS is much broader than in ovarian cancer,
and the occurrence of possible PNS was higher. This ob-
servation suggests that in some patients with breast cancer,
the relation between the neurologic syndrome and this
very common tumor may be coincidental.

Patient 1 was a 47-year-old woman
who presented with a subacute, severe pancerebellar syn-
drome. Brain magnetic resonance (MR) was normal and
CSF analysis showed 40 white cells. Two months later, an
adenocarcinoma of probable breast origin was demon-
strated in an axillary adenopathy. Four years later, she was
tumor free but very disabled from the cerebellar syndrome.
Patient 2 was a 42-year-old woman who developed a severe
cerebellar syndrome 1 month after diagnosis of breast can-
cer. Brain MR was normal and CSF analysis showed 10
white cells. Two years later, she was tumor free and neuro-
logically stable. 
Among the other 5 patients, 4 presented a favorable
evolution related to treatment of the tumor (see Table 2,

Patients 4, 5, 6, 7). These patients had a mild to moderate
cerebellar syndrome weeks to months before the diagno-
sis of breast cancer. They all had normal MR, and the cere-
bellar syndrome improved after removal of the tumor.
Patient 3 (see Table 2) was considered to be possibly para-
neoplastic as she did not improve after tumor treatment.
She had cerebellar atrophy in the initial MR and the clin-
ical picture was similar to that of idiopathic cerebellar de-
generation. 
Sensory-predominant neuropathy
We included in this group 17 (18%) patients in whom
sensory symptoms were the initial complaint and re-
mained isolated or clearly predominant during most of the
clinical course. Patients who showed minor motor weak-
ness or only neurophysiologic motor involvement were in-
cluded in this group. Five patients were positive for Hu-ab
(3 breast, 2 ovary), 2 had amphyphisin-ab (2 breast), 1 had
an atypical antibody (ovary), and 9 had no detectable
antibodies (7 breast, 1 ovary, 1 cervix). The clinical picture
of those patients with Hu-ab, atypical antibody, and
amphiphysin-ab resembled that of patients with Hu-ab,
small cell lung cancer, and sensory neuropathy with pre-
dominant involvement of vibratory and joint position
senses and asymmetric onset (41). The serum of the patient
with the atypical antibody immunoreacted with the neu-
ronal cytoplasm in a pattern different from that described
in a patient with chronic, asymmetric, ataxic sensory neu-
ropathy and breast cancer, whose serum reacted with the
posterior gray horn of the spinal cord (30). All the seropos-
itive patients had an isolated sensory neuropathy with clin-
ical features (asymmetric onset, early involvement of
hands, sensory ataxia) and electromyography (EMG) fea-
tures (absent sensory nerve action potentials with normal
motor nerve conduction velocities in the 5 studies re-
viewed) compatible with primary involvement of the dor-
sal root ganglia (neuronopathy) (13).
The clinical picture and evolution of the 9 seronega-
tive patients was heterogeneous (Table 3). Five patients
(see Table 3, Patients 1, 5, 6, 7, 8) had a large ﬁber sensory
neuropathy with predominant gait ataxia. Four of them
had atypical features for seropositive sensory neuropathy,
2 patients improved, another developed a severe motor
deﬁcit over the ensuing years, and 1 patient had a demy-
elinating neuropathy. Two patients (see Table 3, Patients 3
and 4) presented with paresthesias and itching in the lower
limbs 5 and 9 months before breast cancer was diagnosed
(46). Lastly, Patients 2 and 9 were considered to have pos-
sible paraneoplastic sensory neuropathy because they had
less speciﬁc sensory symptoms (numbness and paresthe-
sias) and did not improve after treatment of the tumor.
Sensorimotor neuropathy
Four patients (4.3%) presented with peripheral neu-
ropathy and predominant motor impairment considered to
be possible PNS associated with breast cancer. Two patients
developed an acute sensorimotor neuropathy fulﬁlling the
criteria for Guillain Barré syndrome, 1 coincident with and
the other 4 months after diagnosis of breast cancer. Two pa-
tients presented a neuropathy with the features of chronic id-
iopathic demyelinating polyneuropathy 9 months before
and 5 months after the diagnosis of breast cancer, respec-
tively. EMG studies suggested a chronic demyelinating
polyradiculoneuropathy in both patients, and a nerve biopsy
performed in 1 demonstrated inﬂammatory and demyelin-

segments.text:
Opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome
Four patients presented with opsoclonus-myoclonus
syndrome. Three patients had breast cancer (2 with Ri-ab)
and 1 ovarian carcinoma. No clinical differences were ob-
served between Ri-ab-negative and Ri-ab-positive patients
with breast cancer. The patient with ovarian cancer devel-
oped opsoclonus without myoclonus 2 months after tumor
diagnosis and after a second cycle of carboplatin, taxol,
and topotecan. The syndrome did not improve and the pa-
tient died from tumor progression 4 months later.
Other neurologic syndromes
Seven patients were considered to have deﬁnitive
PNS associated with breast cancer. Three patients pre-
sented with multifocal involvement of the nervous system
(encephalomyelitis) associated with Ri-ab. Two of them
had a predominant brainstem syndrome with ophthal-
moparesis, dysarthria, tremor, and axial or pancerebellar
syndrome but no opsoclonus. Dorsal bulboprotuberantial,
bilateral, and symmetric hyperintense lesions on T2-
weighted MR images were observed in 1 of the patients.
The third Ri-ab-positive patient presented with a progres-
sive paraparesia with abolished deep tendon reﬂexes and
a T9 sensory level. She subsequently developed weakness
in the upper limbs, urinary incontinence, dysarthria, and
postural tremor in the head and both arms. EMG showed
denervation in the 4 limbs without bulbar involvement.
Spinal and brain MR were normal. A breast adenocarci-
noma was diagnosed 8 months after the onset of neuro-
logic symptoms. 
Two patients had cancer-associated retinopathy.
Antirecoverin or other antiretinal antibodies were not
measured. One patient developed a typical stiff-person
syndrome (positive for amphiphysin-ab, negative for
GAD-ab), and another presented with limbic encephalitis
deﬁned by clinical and MR features 3 months before the
diagnosis of breast cancer. 
Lastly, 3 seronegative patients with breast cancer
were considered as possible paraneoplastic. Two had
amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. The third patient presented
a subacute cerebellar syndrome with multicranial nerve in-
volvement (right VI and VII and bilateral XII nerve
palsies) and bilateral Babinski sign. An axillary lymph
node biopsy revealed an adenocarcinoma 2 months after
the onset of the neurologic symptoms. Distal paresthesias
and amyotrophy appeared during evolution, and elec-
trophysiologic studies revealed an axonal sensory-
predominant neuropathy. She did not improve after treat-
ment of the tumor.
In summary, all patients with gynecologic cancer
presented with deﬁnitive PNS, and onconeural antibodies
were diagnosed in 93% of them. In contrast, 20% of PNSs
associated with breast cancer were deﬁned as possible and
the incidence of onconeural antibodies was 51%, exclud-
ing the 2 patients with paraneoplastic retinopathy in whom
antiretinal antibodies were not analyzed.
